meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The story of the human race is the story of men and women selling themselves short'?
meta.ogDescription: Credited to Abraham Maslow, unsourced in his own work. Wikiquote traces it only to a 1993 paperback. What he actually wrote was different.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: 1908–1970 · American psychologist, founder of humanistic psychology
answer.sourceLine: Widely credited to Maslow and squarely in line with his life’s argument — but no book, lecture transcript or letter containing this wording has been produced. The earliest citation on record is a 1993 motivational paperback, published after his death; what Maslow demonstrably wrote is a differently worded sentence in Toward a Psychology of Being.

source.heading: What can actually be cited

docMeta.dd: Jim Whitt, Road Signs for Success (1993), p. 61 — per Wikiquote
Princeton, NJ: D. Van Nostrand, 1962; 2nd ed., Van Nostrand Reinhold, 1968 — sentence in the Introduction, p. 4

source.excerpt: This inner nature, as much as we know of it so far, seems not to be intrinsically or primarily or necessarily evil… Human nature is not nearly as bad as it has been thought to be. In fact it can be said that the possibilities of human nature have customarily been sold short.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ places the line in its “Attributed” section, citing only Jim Whitt’s Road Signs for Success (1993), p. 61 — a secondary source, published after Maslow’s death.

The same Wikiquote page carries a separate, sourced Maslow sentence on the identical theme, credited to Toward a Psychology of Being; a scan of the book’s Introduction ↗ confirms the wording — “the possibilities of human nature have customarily been sold short” — on p. 4 of the second edition.
The book itself is catalogued at the Internet Archive ↗ as the 1962 Van Nostrand first edition, Princeton, New Jersey; the Whitt paperback is catalogued at Open Library ↗.

Quote Investigator has published no study of this line, and searches of Maslow’s published books turned up no printing of the popular wording — which is why it stays at attributed rather than verified.
source.excerptNote: This is the sentence Maslow demonstrably wrote — from the Introduction, ‘Toward a Psychology of Health,’ p. 4 of the second edition. The popular one-liner is not this sentence and has no located source of its own.
source.rightsNote: Rights cannot be settled because the work containing this exact wording has never been identified. What is certain is that nothing here is public domain: Maslow published from the 1930s until his death in 1970, so any text of his carrying the line would postdate the 1931 US cut-off, and the documented cousin sentence sits in Toward a Psychology of Being (1962; 2nd ed. 1968), which remains in copyright. Treat the line as unsourced and quote it sparingly with attribution.

author.name: Abraham Maslow
author.kicker: The man who thought we underrate ourselves
author.heading: Who was Abraham Maslow?
author.bio: Abraham Maslow was the American psychologist who insisted that his field had learned everything it knew from the sick and almost nothing from the well. Against the Freudian and behaviourist mainstream he built a “third force” psychology of growth, peak experience and self-actualization, set out in Motivation and Personality (1954) and Toward a Psychology of Being (1962). He taught at Brooklyn College and then Brandeis, and died in 1970, a year before The Farther Reaches of Human Nature appeared.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest citation located: Jim Whitt, Road Signs for Success (J. Whitt & Co., 1993), 61, as recorded in Wikiquote’s “Attributed” section. No primary Maslow source found. Compare Abraham H. Maslow, Toward a Psychology of Being, 2nd ed. (New York: Van Nostrand Reinhold, 1968), Introduction, 4.

copyAttribution: Attributed to Abraham Maslow (1908–1970). No primary source located; the earliest citation found is Jim Whitt, "Road Signs for Success" (1993), p. 61. Maslow's documented version, in "Toward a Psychology of Being," reads: "the possibilities of human nature have customarily been sold short." Via Quotle.info

misattribution.heading: The sourcing problem
misattribution.intro: Nobody else is claiming this sentence, so the trouble is not a rival author. It is thinner than that, and harder to fix: no edition, transcript or letter of Maslow’s has ever been produced that contains it.

items.why: Wikiquote ↗ files the line in its “Attributed” section and cites one source for it: p. 61 of this motivational paperback, published in 1993. Maslow died in 1970. Open Library’s record ↗ lists it under the J. Whitt & Co. imprint.

items.who: Abraham Maslow, Toward a Psychology of Being
items.why: What Maslow verifiably wrote is close in sense and quite different in shape: “Human nature is not nearly as bad as it has been thought to be. In fact it can be said that the possibilities of human nature have customarily been sold short.” It appears in the Introduction, ‘Toward a Psychology of Health’ ↗, p. 4 of the second edition.

The sites that put this line in front of most readers carry it bare — no book, no page, no date, and in places a stray year that nothing supports. A quotation that circulates for decades without a single page reference is one that probably entered circulation through talks and posters rather than print.

misattribution.truthLine: Maslow may well have said it; it is his idea, in something like his idiom. But until an edition, a lecture transcript or a letter is produced, the honest label is attributed — and the sentence that can actually be cited is the one in Toward a Psychology of Being ↗.

context.heading: Why the line lands
lead: Maslow’s whole career was one long argument that psychology had built its picture of humanity out of the wrong sample. It studied the broken, the anxious and the institutionalised, then generalised. His counter-move was to study the people who were flourishing — and what he concluded was that our estimate of what a person can be had been set far too low.

So the popular one-liner is not out of character; it is the argument boiled down to a bumper sticker. The catch is that the boiling appears to have been done by somebody else. The version that carries a page number reads: “Human nature is not nearly as bad as it has been thought to be. In fact it can be said that the possibilities of human nature have customarily been sold short.”
detailsBody: The documented sentence is a claim about a discipline: psychology has sold human nature short. The circulating version relocates the failure inside the individual — men and women selling themselves short — which is what makes it quotable on a motivational poster and useless as a citation.

That shift is exactly the kind of drift that happens when a line travels through speeches and seminars before it reaches print. It is also why the trail runs cold: there is no edition to check, because the sentence in circulation may never have been an edition’s sentence.
context.pull: Maslow’s documented sentence is about the possibilities of human nature. The famous one is about you.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote lists "The story of the human race is the story of men and women selling themselves short" in its Attributed section, citing Jim Whitt, Road Signs for Success (1993), p. 61.

The same Wikiquote page carries, in its sourced 1960s section, "Human nature is not nearly as bad as it has been thought to be... In fact it can be said that the possibilities of human nature have customarily been sold short," credited to Toward a Psychology of Being (1962).

This PDF of Toward a Psychology of Being, second edition (copyright 1968, Van Nostrand Reinhold), contains in its Introduction 'Toward a Psychology of Health', p. 4: "Human nature is not nearly as bad as it has been thought to be. In fact it can be said that the possibilities of human nature have customarily been sold short." It does not contain the popular one-liner.
Internet Archive catalogues this item as the 1962 Van Nostrand edition of Maslow's Toward a Psychology of Being, published in Princeton, N.J., and marks it access-restricted.
Open Library holds a record for Road Signs for Success by Jim Whitt, published by J. Whitt & Co.

Wikipedia gives Abraham Maslow's dates as April 1, 1908 - June 8, 1970, describes him as an American psychologist affiliated with Brandeis and Brooklyn College, and dates Motivation and Personality to 1954, Toward a Psychology of Being to 1962 (2nd ed. 1968) and The Farther Reaches of Human Nature to 1971.
